frontmatter_description: Direct-route macro for scenes where an utterance must be judged by its truth status, selective wording, and misleading effect.
title: Lies, Half-Truths, and Misdirection
use_when: Use when the scene centers on whether a speaker lied, told a half-truth, omitted crucial facts, or tried to mislead with wording.
Use when the key question is whether the utterance is literally true, false, or technically true but deceptive.
Use when the listener's mistaken belief is caused by what was said, what was left out, or how the message was framed.
Use when truth value and speaker motive are both relevant to the answer.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the main issue is indirect meaning without deception, such as a request, warning, complaint, refusal, or invitation.
Do not use when the main issue is audience adaptation, persuasion style, or choosing what to say to a listener.
Do not use when the main issue is preference conflict, negotiation, or joint decision making.
Do not use when the main issue is guilt, shame, blame, or responsibility rather than truthfulness or misleading wording.
decision_variable: how an utterance operates across truth value, motive, and misleading effect
direct_route_rule: Route immediately when truth status or wording motive under partial disclosure is central.
trigger_checklist: The scene asks whether the statement is true, false, or only partially true.
The speaker may know more than they say and may be withholding key facts.
The wording is chosen to create a false impression, not just to be polite or indirect.
A listener is meant to believe something incorrect or incomplete.
The answer depends on both content and communicative intent.
workflow: Identify the literal content of the utterance.
Check the actual facts in the scene.
Check what the speaker knew or intended at the moment of speaking.
Decide whether the utterance is false, technically true but misleading, or true and nondeceptive.
If the question asks why it was said that way, answer in terms of concealment, cover, bluff, or misdirection.
If a narrower communication or relationship skill is actually the main issue, exit this macro.

special_case.title: Technically true but misleading
special_case.rule: If the words are factually correct but are chosen to push the listener toward the wrong conclusion, treat the scene as misdirection rather than ordinary indirect speech.

worked_example.scene: A manager asks whether a report is finished. The employee says, 'It is on my desk,' but has not actually completed it and knows the manager will assume it is done.
worked_example.question: Was the employee being truthful?
worked_example.answer_logic: The utterance may be literally true about location, but it is selected to mislead about completion status. The correct classification is deceptive misdirection, not simple indirect communication.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to macro-07 if the utterance is mainly an indirect request, warning, complaint, refusal, reminder, or invitation with no truth-status issue.
Exit to macro-09 if the scene is mainly about tailoring a message to a listener's knowledge, motive, or resistance.
Exit to macro-17 if the scene is mainly about social repair, apology, or relationship damage after the deception.
Exit to macro-01 / macro-02 if the main question is only who believes what, without any deception or selective disclosure in the utterance itself.
Add micro-18 when the listener's belief turns on the source's reliability rather than the speaker's wording.
Add micro-37 to classify literal truth value (true / false / partial).
Add micro-38 when truthful wording produces a misleading inference.
Add micro-39 when the speaker's social motive (cover, save face, bluff) drives wording choice.
Add micro-45 when long-run reputation for honesty is the deciding factor.

references.route_signal: The scene asks whether a speaker lied, told a half-truth, gave a cover story, or used wording to create a false impression.
hard_boundary: Ordinary indirect meaning without deception is not enough.
Pure persuasion without deception is not enough.
Pure preference or negotiation scenes are not enough.
Emotion or blame scenes are not enough unless deception is the core.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not collapse every vague or polite statement into a lie.
Do not treat every misleading listener belief as intentional deception if the utterance is simply indirect.
Do not answer from surface wording alone without checking reality and speaker knowledge.
common_failure_modes: Calling a polite hint a lie when the speaker only meant an indirect request or warning.
Missing a half-truth because the literal words are factually correct.
Focusing on listener misunderstanding while ignoring the speaker's intent.
Using relationship or emotion logic when the key issue is truthfulness.

minimal_pair.case: A person says, 'I already handled it,' meaning only that they sent one email, while knowing the other person will think the whole job is done.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The utterance is technically true but selected to mislead through selective disclosure, which is the macro's signature half-truth pattern.

minimal_pair.case: A guest says, 'It is quite warm in here,' while looking at the closed window, and is clearly making a polite request rather than misleading anyone.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This is a near miss: the utterance is indirect, but truth value is not in question and no false impression of fact is created, so it routes to macro-07 instead.

boundary_stress_test: If the utterance is true but still deceptive, stay in this macro.
If the utterance is indirect but not deceptive, leave this macro.
If the main issue is whether the listener should infer a request or warning, leave this macro.
If the main issue is whether the listener should trust the speaker's reliability over time, consider a trust or relationship macro instead.
references.generalization_note: This macro covers direct lies, strategic omission, bluffing, cover stories, and technically true statements that are designed to mislead, so long as truth status and misleading effect are central.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A speaker says something false, partially true, or carefully framed to create a false belief in the listener.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: A speaker says an indirect request or warning that is not meant to mislead about facts.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A speaker adapts the message to the listener's needs, but the main issue is persuasion or clarity rather than deception.

notes: This is a direct scene prototype, not just a micro bundle.
Use micro-18, micro-37, micro-38, micro-39, and micro-45 only for repair, diagnosis, or explanation when needed.
The core answer logic is: compare words, facts, and speaker intent; then classify the utterance by truthfulness and misleading effect.
core_question: how an utterance operates across truth value, motive, and misleading effect
